raw_case_text:
A 5-year-old premorbidly normal boy presented to the current center with recurrent episodes of headache for last 6 months. First episode occurred 6 months back and the second episode 2 months prior to the current episode. Both the episodes lasted for around 1 week. In this episode, he was symptomatic for 3 days. All three times, including the current episode, his presenting complaints were continuous, generalized, throbbing, moderate to severe intensity headache associated with transient paresthesias (in the bilateral hands and thighs, which lasted for hours to days), getting partially relieved by medications and occasionally associated with non-projectile vomiting. These were not accompanied by any visual or auditory aura (photophobia or phonophobia). The previous two episodes were treated at a different center as meningitis based on CSF reports where he was hospitalized and received parenteral antibiotics, mannitol, and dexamethasone for 2-3 weeks. All three episodes were preceded by a viral prodrome 2-3 weeks before. There was no associated altered sensorium, seizures, cranial nerve palsies, flaccidity or tightness of limbs, abnormal involuntary movements, features suggestive of inco-ordination or bowel bladder disturbances. Fever was absent in all the episodes. There was a significant family history in the form of migraine like headache episodes in the grandmother and sister.
His vital parameters, general physical and systemic examination were essentially normal. His fundus examination did not reveal any feature suggestive of papilledema.
His baseline hematological (hemogram with peripheral smear) and biochemical (serum electrolytes, blood sugar, liver and kidney function tests) investigations were normal. His CSF analysis revealed 60 lymphocytes with normal protein and sugar. Similar CSF findings were also seen in the first two episodes [Table 1]. Analysis of CSF for herpes simplex virus and tubercular polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were negative. Serological tests for Lymes disease and Brucellosis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), anti-nuclear and anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and spine with contrast, magnetic resonance (MR) angiography, and venography study were normal.
Based on the clinical database of recurrent episodes of headache, transient sensory symptoms in form of paresthesias, absence of fever, and normal neurological examination with characteristic CSF picture and normal neuroimaging, diagnosis of HaNDL was made.
Child was started on antimigraine prophylaxis with flunarizine (5 mg/day) in view of strong family history. He became asymptomatic over next 1 week and was discharged. He has not had any recurrence in the last 8 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy presented with a 3-day history of continuous, severe generalized throbbing headache, transient bilateral hand and thigh paresthesias, and non-projectile vomiting, representing his third similar episode in 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A premorbidly healthy 5-year-old boy experienced three stereotypical 1-week episodes over 6 months (6 months prior, 2 months prior, and 3 days prior to current admission) of continuous moderate-to-severe throbbing headache accompanied by transient bilateral hand and thigh paresthesias (lasting hours to days) and occasional non-projectile vomiting, each preceded 2-3 weeks earlier by a viral prodrome. During the first two episodes, he had been hospitalized at an outside center and treated for 2-3 weeks with parenteral antibiotics, mannitol, and dexamethasone for presumed meningitis based on CSF lymphocytosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Two prior hospitalizations (6 months and 2 months earlier) for identical headache/paresthesia episodes with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. Strong family history of migraine-like headaches in his grandmother and sister.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe throbbing headache, transient bilateral hand/thigh paresthesias, non-projectile vomiting, and preceding viral prodrome; negative for fever, photophobia, phonophobia, visual/auditory aura, seizures, altered sensorium, focal motor weakness, ataxia, or sphincter disturbance.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile with normal vital signs; normal general, systemic, neurological, and funduscopic examinations (no papilledema).
objective.routine_investigations: Normal CBC with peripheral smear, serum electrolytes, blood glucose, and liver and renal function tests. Serologic tests for Lyme disease, brucellosis, and HIV were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: ANA and ANCA negative. Lumbar puncture across all three episodes demonstrated isolated lymphocytic pleocytosis (current episode: 60 lymphocytes/mm3) with normal CSF protein and glucose, and negative CSF HSV PCR and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR. Contrast-enhanced brain and spine MRI, MR angiography, and MR venography were completely normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Negative viral, tubercular, Lyme, Brucella, and autoimmune workups junto with recurrent stereotypical attacks of migraine-like headache, transient sensory deficits, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal neuroimaging, and absence of fever confirmed the syndrome of transient Headache and Neurological Deficits with cerebrospinal fluid Lymphocytosis (HaNDL). Started on oral flunarizine prophylaxis (5 mg/day), becoming asymptomatic within 1 week and remaining recurrence-free over 8 months of follow-up.
